core: Demand as the whole relationship between price and quantity demanded (a schedule/curve), not a single amount
The law of demand: price and quantity demanded move inversely, ceteris paribus, giving a downward-sloping curve
Why the curve slopes down: substitution effect, income effect, diminishing marginal utility (briefly)
Quantity demanded (a point) vs demand (the whole curve)
Movement along the curve (own-price change) vs a shift of the curve (determinant change)
Determinants that shift demand: income (normal vs inferior goods), prices of substitutes and complements, tastes, expectations, number of buyers
supporting: Demand schedule (table) and demand curve (graph with quantity on the horizontal axis, price on the vertical)
Ceteris paribus assumption and its role
outOfScope: Market equilibrium / how price is determined (own topic — hand off)
Full consumer-choice / utility-maximization theory (own topic — utility kept light here)

claims.claim: Demand is the relationship between price and the quantity consumers are willing and able to buy at each price; quantity demanded is the specific amount bought at one particular price. 'Demand' refers to the whole curve and 'quantity demanded' to a single point on it.

The law of demand holds that, all else equal (ceteris paribus), a rise in a good's price decreases the quantity demanded and a fall in price increases it, so demand curves slope downward from left to right.
A demand schedule is a table showing quantity demanded at each price; a demand curve is its graph, conventionally drawn with quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical axis.

A change in a good's own price causes a movement ALONG its demand curve (a change in quantity demanded); a change in a non-price determinant causes a SHIFT of the whole curve (a change in demand), meaning a different quantity is demanded at every price.

Determinants that shift demand include income (for a normal good, higher income shifts demand right; for an inferior good, higher income shifts it left), prices of related goods (substitutes and complements), tastes/preferences, expectations about future prices, and the number of buyers/population.

The downward slope reflects the substitution effect (when a good's price rises relative to others, buyers switch toward now-cheaper substitutes) and the income effect (a higher price lowers the purchasing power of income, reducing purchases of a normal good).

Diminishing marginal utility means each additional unit consumed adds less extra satisfaction than the last; because later units are worth less to the buyer, they are purchased only at lower prices, reinforcing the downward-sloping demand relationship.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 3.1: Demand, Supply, and Equilibrium in Markets for Goods and Services
sourceRecords.provider: OpenStax, Rice University (Steven A. Greenlaw, David Shapiro, Daniel MacDonald)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports: demand as 'the amount of some good or service consumers are willing and able to purchase at each price'; quantity demanded as the units purchased at a specific price; the distinction that 'demand refers to the curve and quantity demanded refers to a (specific) point on the curve'; the law of demand (a rise in price almost always decreases quantity demanded, ceteris paribus); the demand schedule (a table of quantity demanded at each price); and the demand curve sloping down from left to right with quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 confirmed on the book's introduction page; treated REFERENCE_ONLY, original prose only.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 3.2: Shifts in Demand and Supply for Goods and Services
sourceRecords.provider: OpenStax, Rice University (Steven A. Greenlaw, David Shapiro, Daniel MacDonald)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports: a change in a good's price causes a movement along its demand curve, while a shift 'happens when a change in some economic factor (other than price) causes a different quantity to be demanded at every price'; determinants that shift demand — income (normal vs inferior goods, e.g. generic groceries as inferior), tastes/preferences (per-capita U.S. chicken consumption rose ~1980-2021), prices of related goods (substitutes and complements, e.g. golf clubs and golf balls), number of buyers/population, and expectations of future prices (stocking up when a price is expected to rise). CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; treated REFERENCE_ONLY, original prose only.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Microeconomics 3e, Section 6.2: How Changes in Income and Prices Affect Consumption Choices
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports the 'why' behind the downward slope: the substitution effect (a price change gives consumers an incentive to consume less of the relatively more expensive good and more of the relatively cheaper one) and the income effect (a higher price reduces the buying power of income, leading to buying less of a normal good); both effects can occur simultaneously and typically reduce consumption of a good whose price rises. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; treated REFERENCE_ONLY, original prose only.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Microeconomics 3e, Section 6.1: Consumption Choices
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports diminishing marginal utility: the additional (marginal) utility decreases with each unit added, so 'each additional movie brings a smaller gain in utility than the previous one' (T-shirt example: first shirt 22 utils, fourth 18 utils). Used only for the light utility rationale behind the downward slope; full utility-maximization theory is out of scope (consumer-choice topic). CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; treated REFERENCE_ONLY, original prose only.
